Question Prompt Passage

Passage A

Research concerning happiness and wealth reveals a paradox: at any one time richer people report higher levels of happiness than poorer people in the same society report, and yet over time advanced societies have not grown happier as they have grown richer. Apparently, people are comparing their income with some norm, and that norm must be rising along with actual income. Two phenomena—habituation and rivalry—push up the norm.

When our living standards increase, we love it initially but then we adjust and it makes little difference. For example, if we ask people with different incomes what income they consider sufficient, the "required income" correlates strongly with their actual income: a rise in actual income causes a roughly equivalent rise in required income. We can also look at reported happiness over time. Job satisfaction depends little on the absolute level of wages but rises if wages rapidly increase.

We do not have the same experience with other aspects of our lives. We do not foresee how we adjust to material possessions, so we overinvest in acquiring them, at the expense of leisure.

Now consider the phenomenon of rivalry. In a study conducted by Solnick and Hemenway, people were asked to choose between two options, with all prices held constant:

A. You earn $50,000 a year while everyone else earns $25,000;

B. You earn $100,000 a year while others make $200,000.

The majority chose the first. They were happy to be poorer, provided their relative position improved.

And indeed, how people compare to their "reference group"—those most like them—is crucial for happiness. In East Germany, for example, living standards have soared since 1990, but the level of happiness has plummeted because people now compare themselves with West Germans, rather than with people in other Soviet bloc countries.

Passage B

Does the Solnick and Hemenway study mean that we care most about one-upmanship? Perhaps out of our primeval past comes the urge to demonstrate our superiority in order to help ensure mating prospects, keeping our genetic lines going. Still programmed like this, we get unexplainable pleasure from having a bigger house than our neighbors.

This theory may sound good and is commonly heard, but it is not the explanation best supported by the evidence. Rather, the data show that earning more makes people happier because relative prosperity makes them feel that they are successful, that they have created value.

If two people feel equally successful, they will be equally happy even if their incomes differ greatly. Of course, people who earn more generally view themselves as successful. But it is the success—not the money per se—that provides the happiness. We use material wealth to show not just that we are prosperous, but that we are prosperous because we create value.

What scholars often portray as an ignoble tendency—wanting to have more than others—is really evidence of a desire to create value. Wanting to create value benefits society. It is a bonus that it also brings happiness.

Passage A

Research concerning happiness and wealth reveals a paradox: at any one time richer people report higher levels of happiness than poorer people in the same society report, and yet over time advanced societies have not grown happier as they have grown richer. Apparently, people are comparing their income with some norm, and that norm must be rising along with actual income. Two phenomena—habituation and rivalry—push up the norm.

It is generally believed that while in some cases government should intervene to protect people from risk—by imposing air safety standards, for example—in other cases, such as mountain climbing, the onus should be on the individual to protect himself or herself. In the eyes of the public at large, the demarcation between the two kinds of cases has mainly to do with whether the risk in question is incurred voluntarily. This distinction between voluntary and involuntary risk may in fact be the chief difference between lay and expert judgments about risk. Policy experts tend to focus on aggregate lives at stake; laypeople care a great deal whether a risk is undertaken voluntarily. However, judgments about whether a risk is "involuntary" often stem from confusion and selective attention, and the real reason for such judgments frequently lies in an antecedent judgment of some other kind. They are thus of little utility in guiding policy decisions.

First, it is not easy to determine when a risk is voluntarily incurred. Although voluntariness may be entirely absent in the case of an unforeseeable collision with an asteroid, with most environmental, occupational, and other social risks, it is not an all-or-nothing matter, but rather one of degree. Risks incurred by airline passengers are typically thought to be involuntary, since passengers have no control over whether a plane is going to crash. But they can choose airlines on the basis of safety records or choose not to fly. In characterizing the risks as involuntary, people focus on a small part of a complex interaction, not the decision to fly, but the accident when it occurs.

Second, people often characterize risks as "voluntary" when they do not approve of the purpose for which people run the risks. It is unlikely that people would want to pour enormous taxpayer resources into lowering the risks associated with skydiving, even if the ratio of dollars spent to lives saved were quite good. By contrast, people would probably not object to spending enormous resources on improving the safety of firefighters, even though the decision to become a firefighter is voluntary. In short, there is no special magic in notions like "voluntary" and "involuntary." Therefore, regulatory policy should be guided by a better understanding of the factors that underlie judgments about voluntariness.

In general, the government should attempt to save as many lives as it can, subject to the limited public and private resources devoted to risk reduction. Departures from this principle should be justified not by invoking the allegedly voluntary or involuntary nature of a particular risk, but rather by identifying the more specific considerations for which notions of voluntariness serve as proxies.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: In general, whether people characterize a risk as voluntary or involuntary depends on whether they approve of the purpose for which the risk is taken.
choices.rationale: This is one of the flaws in voluntariness considerations that the author brings up, but it’s too narrow to encompass the main point. Rather, the main point is that the government shouldn’t use considerations of voluntariness to shape policy about protecting people from risks, and should instead shape such policy around saving as many people as possible.

choices.text: Decisions about government intervention to protect people from risks should be based primarily on how many lives can be saved rather than on whether the risks are considered voluntary.
choices.rationale: This sums up the main point. The first paragraph states the thesis, that the government shouldn’t use considerations of voluntariness to shape risk intervention policy. The second and third paragraph further explains the author’s reasoning, and the last paragraph asserts that the government should instead shape policy around saving as many lives as it can.

choices.text: Though laypeople may object, experts should be the ones to determine whether the risk incurred in a particular action is voluntary or involuntary.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. The author believes that judgments about voluntariness are flawed, and are thus “of little utility in guiding policy decisions.” Whether or not experts or laypeople are doing the judging is irrelevant—and in fact, the author says that it’s mostly laypeople who care about voluntariness in the first place, while policy experts “tend to focus on aggregate lives at stake” (first paragraph).

choices.text: Public-policy decisions related to the protection of society against risk are difficult to make because of the difficulty of distinguishing risks incurred voluntarily from those incurred involuntarily.
choices.rationale: The author neither states nor implies that public-policy decisions related to the protection of society against risk are difficult to make in general, let alone that distinguishing voluntariness from involuntariness is the reason—rather, the author argues that such decisions should not be based on voluntariness, and should instead be based on saving as many lives as possible. The difficulty of the decision-making is out of the scope of the passage.

choices.text: People who make judgments about the voluntary or involuntary character of a risk are usually unaware of the complicated motivations that lead people to take risks.
choices.rationale:
First, this choice is too narrow. Purposes for taking risks are mentioned in paragraph three, but they are related to only one of the author's reasons (for why judgments about voluntariness are often really about something else). So this choice doesn't account for the reason discussed in paragraph two, and, more importantly, it doesn't account for the author's overall argument about what should guide policy decisions.
Also, this choice distorts the content of the passage. In paragraph three, the author suggests that people's judgement about voluntariness is influenced by whether they approve of the purpose for which people take risks. But the author does not suggest that people are "unaware" of those purposes.

choices.text: traveling in outer space
choices.rationale: Though it’s not discussed in the passage, given that laypeople think skydiving involves voluntarily risk, they would likely think that traveling in outer space is a voluntary-risk activity as well.

choices.text: participating in skydiving
choices.rationale: Skydiving is considered a voluntary-risk activity by laypeople (third paragraph).

choices.text: serving as a firefighter
choices.rationale: According to the passage, laypeople often characterize risks as "voluntary" when they do not approve of the purpose for which people run the risks. Skydiving is contrasted with firefighting in this regard, as skydiving doesn’t have an approved-of purpose, while firefighting does. However it’s still a personal choice to become a firefighter, and therefore the risk assumed is not totally involuntary (i.e., the risk is freely assumed). So if laypeople say that firefighting involves involuntary risk, what they really mean, according to the author, is that the risk is for an approved-of purpose—to put out fires.

choices.text: traveling in airplanes
choices.rationale: The second paragraph states that “risks incurred by airline passengers are typically thought to be involuntary, since passengers have no control over whether a plane is going to crash.” In other words, laypeople generally consider traveling in airplanes as an activity that involves risks that are not freely assumed.

choices.text: climbing mountains
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. In the first paragraph we’re told that laypeople think the government shouldn’t intervene to protect people from risks associated with mountain climbing. So we can infer that laypeople do consider mountain climbing to be an activity that involves freely assumed risk.

It is generally believed that while in some cases government should intervene to protect people from risk—by imposing air safety standards, for example—in other cases, such as mountain climbing, the onus should be on the individual to protect himself or herself. In the eyes of the public at large, the demarcation between the two kinds of cases has mainly to do with whether the risk in question is incurred voluntarily. This distinction between voluntary and involuntary risk may in fact be the chief difference between lay and expert judgments about risk. Policy experts tend to focus on aggregate lives at stake; laypeople care a great deal whether a risk is undertaken voluntarily. However, judgments about whether a risk is "involuntary" often stem from confusion and selective attention, and the real reason for such judgments frequently lies in an antecedent judgment of some other kind. They are thus of little utility in guiding policy decisions.

First, it is not easy to determine when a risk is voluntarily incurred. Although voluntariness may be entirely absent in the case of an unforeseeable collision with an asteroid, with most environmental, occupational, and other social risks, it is not an all-or-nothing matter, but rather one of degree. Risks incurred by airline passengers are typically thought to be involuntary, since passengers have no control over whether a plane is going to crash. But they can choose airlines on the basis of safety records or choose not to fly. In characterizing the risks as involuntary, people focus on a small part of a complex interaction, not the decision to fly, but the accident when it occurs.

Second, people often characterize risks as "voluntary" when they do not approve of the purpose for which people run the risks. It is unlikely that people would want to pour enormous taxpayer resources into lowering the risks associated with skydiving, even if the ratio of dollars spent to lives saved were quite good. By contrast, people would probably not object to spending enormous resources on improving the safety of firefighters, even though the decision to become a firefighter is voluntary. In short, there is no special magic in notions like "voluntary" and "involuntary." Therefore, regulatory policy should be guided by a better understanding of the factors that underlie judgments about voluntariness.

In general, the government should attempt to save as many lives as it can, subject to the limited public and private resources devoted to risk reduction. Departures from this principle should be justified not by invoking the allegedly voluntary or involuntary nature of a particular risk, but rather by identifying the more specific considerations for which notions of voluntariness serve as proxies.
stem: The author's use of the phrase "no special magic" (second to last sentence of the third paragraph) is most likely meant primarily to convey that notions like "voluntary" and "involuntary"

choices.text: do not exhaustively characterize the risks that people commonly face
choices.rationale: The author likely agrees that notions like "voluntary" and "involuntary" don’t exhaustively characterize the risks people commonly face, but that's not the purpose of saying that such notions have “no special magic.” Rather, the author means to convey that we can't rely on judgments about the voluntariness of incurring risk for guidance in shaping policy. Also, in this paragraph, the author isn’t talking about just risks that “people commonly face,” but also risks that are not commonly faced (such as the risks associated with skydiving and firefighting).

choices.text: have been used to intentionally conceal the factors motivating government efforts to protect people from risks
choices.rationale: The author never states or implies that the notions of “voluntary” and “involuntary” have been used to intentionally conceal the factors motivating government efforts to protect people from risk. The author argues that judgments about the voluntariness of taking on risk—a paradigm often favored by laypeople—are flawed, and that they reflect other kinds of judgments (subconsciously) buried within them. But there's never any accusation of intentionally concealing the other factors at play, either on the part of the government, the policy experts, or the laypeople.

choices.text: have no meaning beyond their literal, dictionary definitions
choices.rationale: This is too strong. The author argues that when it comes to incurring risk, notions of “voluntary” and “involuntary” are very flawed—but not that these concepts have no meaning at all beyond their dictionary definitions. Rather, by stating that they have “no special magic” when it comes to policy decisions about risk intervention, the author means to convey that we can't rely on such judgments for guidance.

choices.text: are mistakenly believed to be characteristics that inform people's understanding of the consequences of risk
choices.rationale: The author doesn't use the phrase “no special magic” to say anything about consequences. In fact, the consequences of risk are out of the scope of the passage entirely. Rather, the author means to convey that we can't rely on judgments about the voluntariness of incurring risks to shape policy.

choices.text: provide a flawed mechanism for making public policy decisions relating to risk reduction
choices.rationale: The sentence concludes two paragraphs that each delve into a reason why the voluntariness of incurring risk isn’t a valuable tool for shaping public policy decisions—first, it’s difficult to nail down when a risk is voluntarily incurred in the first place; and second, people often (incorrectly) characterize risks as "voluntary" when they don’t approve of the purpose of taking the risk. Thus, that such judgments are flawed and can’t be used to guide risk-reduction policy is the author’s intention behind saying that these notions have “no special magic.”

stem: The passage most strongly supports the inference that the author believes which one of the following?

choices.text: Whenever an activity involves the risk of loss of human life, the government should intervene to reduce the degree of risk incurred.
choices.rationale: The author argues that risk-reduction policy should be based on saving as many lives as possible, subject to the limited resources devoted to risk reduction (last paragraph). So the author may not believe that an activity that involves the risk of just one or just a few lives merits any government intervention. Hence, we can’t infer that the author would agree with this statement.

choices.text: Some environmental risks are voluntary to a greater degree than others are.
choices.rationale: In the second paragraph, the author argues that “with most environmental, occupational, and other social risks, [voluntariness] is not an all-or-nothing matter, but rather one of degree.” This implies that the author believes there are different degrees of voluntariness involved in environmental risks, with some involving more than others.

choices.text: Policy experts are more likely than laypeople to form an accurate judgment about the voluntariness or involuntariness of an activity.
choices.rationale: The author never implies that policy experts are more accurate in judgments about the voluntariness of risk than laypeople are—in fact, the author states that policy experts tend to “focus on aggregate lives at stake” instead of voluntariness (first paragraph). The author only claims that laypeople care more about voluntariness than experts.

choices.text: The government should increase the quantity of resources devoted to protecting people from risk.
choices.rationale: In the last paragraph, the author writes that “the government should attempt to save as many lives as it can, subject to the limited public and private resources devoted to risk reduction.” The author never argues that these resources aren’t enough and should be increased—just that the government must work within the limits of what resources there are.

choices.text: Government policies intended to reduce risk are not justified unless they comport with most people's beliefs.
choices.rationale: This choice conflicts with the author’s views. The author states that laypeople tend to care deeply about the voluntariness of the risk incurred, but then goes on to argue that such judgments are flawed and shouldn’t be used to guide policy, despite what these laypeople want. So it’s unlikely that the author would agree that policy should comport with most people’s beliefs.

stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's attitude in the passage?

choices.text: chagrin at the rampant misunderstanding of the relative risks associated with various activities
choices.rationale: Chagrin is too strong of a word to describe the author’s attitude in any part of the passage. The author is certainly doubtful of the utility of voluntariness in guiding risk-management policy, and the author focuses on poking holes in the logic of “voluntary” versus “involuntary” risk to prove that point. But “chagrin” implies distress or embarrassment that isn’t there in the author’s (more scholarly) tone.

choices.text: concern that policy guided mainly by laypeople's emphasis on the voluntariness of risk would lead to excessive government regulation
choices.rationale: This is out of scope. The author never expresses any concern about excessive government regulation. In fact, the author doesn’t bring up “excessive” regulation at all, let alone linking it to laypeople's emphasis on the voluntariness of risk.

choices.text: skepticism about the reliability of laypeople's intuitions as a general guide to deciding government risk-management policy
choices.rationale: The author states that laypeople tend to care deeply about whether or not a risk is incurred voluntarily or involuntarily when considering government risk-management policy (first paragraph). However, throughout most the passage, the author argues that their judgments about voluntariness in risk are highly flawed and therefore not useful in shaping policy. The author ultimately comes down on the side of the policy experts, who tend to focus on aggregate lives saved instead. From this, we can infer that the author is skeptical about the reliability of laypeople's intuitions as a general guide to deciding government risk-management policy.

choices.text: conviction that the sole criterion that can justify government intervention to reduce risk is the saving of human lives
choices.rationale: This is too strong. The author says that government risk-reduction policy should focus on saving as many lives as possible, but that when this principle must be deviated from, we should strive to justify the reasoning with something deeper than voluntariness (last paragraph). So the author anticipates needing to deviate from the “aggregate lives saved” principle at some point. Hence, we can’t say the author believes the sole criterion that can justify government intervention to reduce risk is the saving of human lives.

choices.text: eagerness to persuade the reader that policy experts' analysis of risk is distorted by subtle biases
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. The author ultimately comes down in favor of the policy experts’ focus on aggregate lives at stake instead of the voluntariness of the risk incurred. In fact, we can infer that the author believes the laypeople’s analysis of risk is the one distorted by subtle biases.

In an experiment, ten people were asked to taste samples of coffee and rank them. Five of the people were given chocolate with the coffee, and this group subsequently reported that all the coffee samples tasted pretty much the same as one another. Five others tasted coffee only, and they were able to detect differences. Clearly, then, chocolate interferes with one's ability to taste coffee.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the conclusion drawn above?

choices.text: The ten people were randomly assigned to either the group that tasted only coffee or the group that was also given chocolate, although some people had asked to be in the group that received chocolate.
choices.rationale: This could actually strengthen the conclusion in the passage. (A) removes the possibility that the group assignments weren’t random, which would have weakened the experiment. Removing a potential weakener results in a net effect of strengthening a position.

choices.text: Similar results were achieved when the experiment was repeated with a different, larger group of people.
choices.rationale: This could actually strengthen the conclusion in the passage. If the experiment’s results were reproduced with a different, larger group of people, then it’s less likely that the experiment was an anomaly.

choices.text: Chocolate is normally consumed as a solid, whereas coffee is normally consumed as a liquid.
choices.rationale: This comparison doesn’t affect the argument. How chocolate and coffee are normally consumed is irrelevant to whether chocolate interferes with the ability to taste differences in coffee.

choices.text: The five people who were originally given chocolate were asked a week later to taste coffee samples without chocolate, and they still detected no differences between the coffee samples.
choices.rationale: This weakens the conclusion that chocolate interferes with one’s ability to taste coffee. If (D) is true, then the five people (who were originally given chocolate and couldn’t taste the difference among samples of coffee) still couldn’t taste the difference later without chocolate to influence them. That strongly suggests that something else is responsible for their inability to taste the differences—not chocolate.

choices.text: Some subjects who tasted just coffee reported only subtle differences between the coffee samples, while others thought the differences were considerable.
choices.rationale: This comparison doesn’t affect the argument. It remains true that the people in the group that ate chocolate could detect hardly any differences between the coffee samples, so learning about a range of differences among the subjects in the other group is neither helpful nor harmful to the conclusion that chocolate interferes with the ability to taste coffee.

stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning of the residents opposed to building the house?

choices.text: Every possible effort should be made to preserve historic buildings that are well known and well loved.
choices.rationale: The situation in the stimulus is about preserving landscape, not a building, so this answer is out of scope.

choices.text: Communities that seek to preserve undeveloped areas of landscape or historic neighborhoods should purchase those properties for the public trust.
choices.rationale: The stimulus never discusses purchasing land for the public trust, so this answer is out of scope.

choices.text: Artists who choose to represent actual landscapes in their paintings have the right to demand that the owners of the land represented do not significantly alter the landscape.
choices.rationale: The artist in question isn't the one pushing for the preservation of this land—in fact, that painter recently died.

choices.text: The right to build on one's own property is constrained by the artistic and historical interests of the community at large.
choices.rationale: This answer choice provides justification for using artistic and historical interests to oppose building property on someone else's private land, thus strengthening the position of the residents of this community.

choices.text: In historic communities, the building and zoning regulations should prohibit construction that obstructs access to historic sites.
choices.rationale: First, there's no indication that this community is historic (just that it has a historic heritage). Moore: Sunscreen lotions, which are designed to block skin-cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation, do not do so effectively. Many scientific studies have shown that people who have consistently used these lotions develop, on average, as many skin cancers as those who have rarely, if ever, used them.
stem: The reasoning in Moore's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.text: takes for granted that there are no other possible health benefits of using sunscreen lotions other than blocking skin-cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation
choices.rationale: This isn’t a flaw in Moore’s argument, which focuses on how well sunscreen lotions block skin-cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation. Whether sunscreen lotions bring other possible health benefits isn’t relevant to how effectively the lotions prevent skin cancer.

choices.text: fails to distinguish between the relative number of cases of skin cancer and the severity of those cases in measuring effectiveness at skin cancer prevention
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in Moore’s argument, which addresses the rate at which two groups of people develop skin cancer, period. The severity of the cancer isn’t in question here.

choices.text: fails to consider the effectiveness of sunscreen lotions that are not specifically designed to block skin-cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation
choices.rationale: This isn’t a flaw in Moore’s argument, which focuses on how effective sunscreen lotions are that are designed to block skin-cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation. Learning about how effective other sunscreen lotions are wouldn’t resolve any flaws in this argument.

choices.text: relies on evidence regarding the probability of people in different groups developing cancer that, in principle, would be impossible to challenge
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in Moore’s argument, which never addresses the “probability” of people developing cancer—only the rate of people developing cancer. Additionally, it isn’t clear that any of the evidence provided would be “impossible to challenge.”

choices.text: overlooks the possibility that people who consistently use sunscreen lotions spend more time in the sun, on average, than people who do not
choices.rationale:
This describes a flaw in Moore’s argument. Moore makes a comparison in the support between people who have consistently used sunscreen lotions and people who have rarely, if ever, used sunscreen lotions. In order for this argument to work, these two groups would need to be sufficiently comparable.
To put this into a different context, imagine running shoes that advertised themselves as effective because, “the people who consistently wear them run faster than the people who rarely wear them.” What if the people who rarely wear them don’t even run to begin with? In that case, the two groups being compared wouldn’t be on equal ground. Of course the people who rarely wear them don’t run faster—they don’t run at all!
In the same way, it’s possible that the group who used sunscreen consistently already spent more time in the sun than people who didn’t. So, Moore can’t logically compare two groups that are completely different risks of skin cancer to begin with.

choices.text: claiming that the argument is based on a false analogy

stem: Which one of the following statements most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the argument?

choices.text: Biodiversity does not require that all existing species continue to exist.
choices.rationale: This statement expresses the argument’s conclusion, which is in the first sentence. The second sentence explains why not all existing species need to continue existing in order to maintain biodiversity: if a given ecological niche could be filled by species A, B, or C, for example, then only one of these three would need to survive. Because (A) is supported by the second sentence, and doesn’t in turn support any other statements, it’s the argument’s conclusion.

choices.text: There are various ecological niches that must be filled if there is to be life on Earth.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the argument’s conclusion, because it forms part of the support for why biodiversity doesn’t require the survival of every currently existing species.

choices.text: The survival of life on Earth depends upon biodiversity.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the argument’s conclusion. It’s part of the sentence that contains the conclusion (that biodiversity doesn’t require all existing species to survive), but it’s not what the arguer is trying to prove. Nothing in the passage serves to explain why the survival of life on Earth depends upon biodiversity. This statement is something that the arguer addresses and then moves on from.

choices.text: There are many ecological niches that can be filled by more than one species.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the argument’s conclusion, because it forms part of the support for why biodiversity doesn’t require the survival of every currently existing species.

choices.text: The species most indispensable for biodiversity fill more than one ecological niche.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the argument’s conclusion, because nothing about the species “most indispensable for biodiversity” was ever stated anywhere in the passage.

Clinician: Patients with immune system disorders are usually treated with a class of drugs that, unfortunately, increase the patient's risk of developing osteoporosis, a bone-loss disease. So these patients take another drug that helps to preserve existing bone. Since a drug that enhances the growth of new bone cells has now become available, these patients should take this new drug in addition to the drug that helps to preserve existing bone.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the clinician's argument?

choices.text: How large is the class of drugs that increase the risk of developing osteoporosis?
choices.rationale: The answer to this question isn’t useful to know. Whether it’s a large class or a small class of drugs that increase the risk of developing osteoporosis, that doesn’t affect whether patients with immune system disorders should take the new drug.

choices.text: Why are immune system disorders treated with drugs that increase the risk of developing osteoporosis?
choices.rationale: The answer to this question isn’t useful to know. We’re told that patients with immune system disorders are currently treated with these drugs, and it’s reasonable to assume that doctors have a good reason for prescribing these drugs, regardless of the side effects. Knowing (or not knowing) the exact reason doesn’t help us determine whether these patients should take the new drug.

choices.text: Is the new drug more expensive than the drug that helps to preserve existing bone?
choices.rationale: The answer to this question isn’t useful to know. The proposal is that the new drug be taken with the old drug, not instead of it. The comparative costs of these drugs aren’t relevant.

choices.text: How long has the drug that helps to preserve existing bone been in use?
choices.rationale: The answer to this question isn’t useful to know. We’d have to make a lot of assumptions—something we should avoid on Test Day—in order to make (D) be relevant. For example, some students are tempted to assume that longevity of use means that a drug is better, but that isn’t demonstrated.

choices.text: To what extent does the new drug retain its efficacy when used in combination with the other drugs?
choices.rationale: The answer to this question is useful to know in order to evaluate the clinician’s argument. If the new drug doesn’t retain its efficacy when used in combination with the other drugs, then we would be less inclined to agree with the clinician. If, on the other hand, the new drug does retain its efficacy when used in combination with the other drugs, we would be more inclined to agree with the clinician. Remember—we’re not trying to prove or disprove an argument with the answer; we’re looking for the question that would be helpful to know the answer to.

stem: The critic's reasoning most closely conforms to which one of the following principles?

choices.text: A civic building that is located in a downtown area should, if possible, be located on an elevated site.
choices.rationale: This answer doesn't address whether a civic building is successfully serving its purpose, just where it should be built if possible. And since the Critic believes the art museum is successful without mentioning where it's built, she can't believe it's all that relevant. Finally, the image of the "city on the hill" is dismissed as not guaranteeing a truly elevated purpose.

choices.text: A city needs to have civic buildings if it is to have social cohesion.
choices.rationale: This answer sets up civic buildings as a necessary part of creating social cohesion, but it doesn't establish social cohesion as a purpose of civic buildings. This answer is a bit of a reversal of what we're looking for—a principle establishing social cohesion as a necessary element of a successful civic building.

choices.text: A civic building with an elevated purpose should be located on a spectacular site.
choices.rationale: The argument is about whether a civic building serves its purpose, not whether it has an "elevated purpose" and should be on a spectacular site. If anything, in suggesting that the art museum is successful despite being located in the heart of downtown, it's saying that there are factors much more important than the spectacle of the location.

choices.text: The downtown area of a city should be designed in a way that complements the area's civic buildings.
choices.rationale: There's no discussion of how areas of a city should be designed—just what a successful civic building should do, regardless of its location.

choices.text: The purpose of a civic building is to encourage social cohesion and to make a city more alive.
choices.rationale: This answer provides a principle establishing the purpose of civic buildings. The Critic states that the art museum succeeds as a civic building where the concert hall fails because the former encourages social cohesion and makes the city feel alive. If those are the purposes of a civic building, as this answer choice states, then the conclusion holds.

Fluoride enters a region's groundwater when rain dissolves fluoride-bearing minerals in the soil. In a recent study, researchers found that when rainfall, concentrations of fluoride-bearing minerals, and other relevant variables are held constant, fluoride concentrations in groundwater are significantly higher in areas where the groundwater also contains a high concentration of sodium.
stem: Which one of the following can most reasonably be concluded on the basis of the researchers' findings?

choices.text: Fluoride-bearing minerals are not the primary source of fluoride found in groundwater.
choices.rationale: The stimulus establishes that these minerals are how fluoride enters the groundwater, so this answer is contradicted.

choices.text: Rainfall does not affect fluoride concentrations in groundwater.
choices.rationale: Incorrect. The relationship in the stimulus held rainfall constant, thus removing it from the equation. Different levels of rainfall could result in different fluoride levels, but the amount of rain has the same effect on those levels.

choices.text: Sodium-bearing minerals dissolve at a faster rate than fluoride-bearing minerals.
choices.rationale: There's no comparison between fluoride levels and sodium levels, just a note that high levels of each go hand in hand.

choices.text: Sodium in groundwater increases the rate at which fluoride-bearing minerals dissolve.
choices.rationale: This answer connects the high sodium levels where there's high fluoride levels when all else is held constant to the means by which fluoride gets into the groundwater. If the only relevant difference between areas with different fluoride levels is sodium, and the source of fluoride in groundwater is dissolved minerals, then the sodium must act to get that fluoride from the minerals faster.

choices.text: Soil that contains high concentrations of sodium-bearing minerals also contains high concentrations of fluoride-bearing minerals.
choices.rationale: High fluoride is correlated with high sodium levels, not the other way around. This answer reverses the relationship.

Fraenger's assertion that the artist Hieronymus Bosch belonged to the Brethren of the Free Spirit, a nonmainstream religious group, is unlikely to be correct. Fraenger's hypothesis explains much of Bosch's unusual subject matter. However, there is evidence that Bosch was a member of a mainstream church, and no evidence that he was a member of the Brethren.
stem: The statement that there is no evidence that Bosch was a member of the Brethren figures in the argument in which one of the following ways?

choices.text: It is a premise that, when combined with the other premises, guarantees the falsity of Fraenger's assertion.
choices.rationale: The argument isn't designed to show the F's hypothesis is wrong but that it is "unlikely to be correct." This answer is too strong.

choices.text: It is used to support the claim that Bosch was a member of a mainstream church.
choices.rationale: While an implication of the argument is that B was a member of a mainstream church, that isn't the main point. Additionally, the statement in question is meant to call into question F's hypothesis that B was in a cult, not that he was in a mainstream church—a subtle difference, but a difference nonetheless.

choices.text: It is used to dispute Fraenger's hypothesis by questioning Fraenger's credibility.
choices.rationale: This answer is describing an ad hominem attack, but there's no questioning of F's credibility. Bringing up reasons to doubt someone's argument isn't questioning their credibility.

choices.text: It is intended to cast doubt on Fraenger's hypothesis by questioning the sufficiency of Fraenger's evidence.
choices.rationale: This answer highlights the role of the statement in question. It's a premise that is used to rebut F's argument by stating that there's no evidence backing it up.

choices.text: It is intended to help show that Bosch's choice of subject matter remains unexplained.
choices.rationale: The author does agree that F's hypothesis explains B's strange subject matter, but she doesn't state that it's the only potential explanation. The argument also isn't designed to establish that the subject matter is, was, or remains unexplained.

stimulus:

Vacuum cleaner salesperson: To prove that this Super XL vacuum cleaner is better than your old vacuum cleaner, I ran your old vacuum once over this dirty carpet. Then I ran the Super XL over the same area. All that dirt that the Super XL picked up is dirt your old vacuum left behind, proving the Super XL is the better vacuum.
stem: The vacuum cleaner salesperson's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it

choices.text: ignores the possibility that dirt remained in the carpet even after the Super XL had been used in the test
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in the salesperson’s argument. The Super XL could still be the superior vacuum, even if it didn’t clean all the dirt in the carpet.

choices.text: takes for granted that the Super XL will still perform better than the old vacuum cleaner when it is the same age as the old vacuum cleaner
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in the salesperson’s argument. The salesperson concludes that the Super XL is the better vacuum than the old vacuum now—presumably in order to convince the vacuum owner that they should replace the old vacuum with the Super XL. How they’ll perform when they’re the same age isn’t relevant.

choices.text: takes for granted that because the Super XL outperforms one vacuum cleaner it is the best vacuum cleaner available
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in the salesperson’s argument. The salesperson never claims that the Super XL is the best vacuum cleaner available, but rather that the Super XL is better than the owner’s current, old vacuum.

choices.text: ignores the possibility that the amount of dirt removed in the test by the old vacuum cleaner is greater than the amount of dirt removed by the Super XL
choices.rationale: This choice tempts some students, but it doesn’t describe a flaw in the salesperson’s argument. The old vacuum could very well have picked up more dirt than the Super XL, just by virtue of having gone first—but this tells us nothing about the quality of the two vacuums. The salesperson’s real flaw is in assuming that the Super XL would have picked up all the original dirt and the leftover dirt that the old vacuum left behind.

choices.text: ignores the possibility that if the Super XL had been used first it would have left behind just as much dirt as did the old vacuum cleaner
choices.rationale:
This describes a flaw in the salesperson’s argument. The salesperson didn’t run a second test—one in which the Super XL was used first and the old vacuum second. The salesperson is assuming that the Super XL would have picked up the amount of dirt that the old vacuum did, plus the extra dirt that the old vacuum left behind. But this isn’t necessarily so.
Think about opening a jar; sometimes, one person tries to open the jar and can’t. When another person successfully opens the jar, the first person sometimes jokes, “I loosened it for you.” But, it’s actually possible that the first person did loosen it ever so slightly, and if they hadn’t done so, the second person may not have been able to open the jar. The same is true with the vacuums in this example. The Super XL was used on a carpet that was already partly cleaned, so it had less of a job to do than the old vacuum did.

Manager: This company's supply chain will develop significant weaknesses unless we make changes to our vendor contracts now. Some will argue that this problem is so far in the future that there is no need to address it today. But that is an irresponsible approach. Just imagine if a financial planner offered the same counsel to a 30-year-old client: "Don't worry, Jane, retirement is 35 years away; you don't need to save anything now." That planner would be guilty of gross malpractice.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the manager's argument?

choices.text: Some people argue that the supply-chain problem is so far in the future that there is no need to address it now.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the manager’s conclusion. This is an assumption of the manager’s argument. The manager refutes the position of those people who argue that the problem is too far in the future to address.

choices.text: It would be irresponsible to postpone changes to the vendor contracts just because the supply chain will not develop weaknesses for a long time.
choices.rationale: This is the manager’s overall conclusion. Some students identify the passage’s first sentence as the conclusion, but note that the support explains why it’s a bad idea to not act on the basis of an event being far off in the future. The support isn’t backing up the claim of the first sentence: why the supply chain will develop significant weaknesses unless the company makes changes. That is something the manager is taking for granted, and they spend no time trying to prove the validity of that claim.

choices.text: If no changes are made to the vendor contracts, the supply chain will eventually develop significant weaknesses.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the manager’s overall conclusion, though it does sound like it could be at first. However, the manager’s support explains why it’s a bad idea to not act on the basis of an event being far off in the future. It isn’t explaining why the supply chain will develop significant weaknesses unless the company makes changes. That is something the manager is taking for granted, and spends no time trying to prove the validity of that claim.

choices.text: In planning to meet its future obligations, a company should follow the same practices that are appropriate for an individual who is planning for retirement.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the manager’s conclusion, because it’s never stated. Just because the manager uses an analogy to prove a point doesn’t mean that the manager thinks the company should follow the same practices as those in the analogy. The point is that it’s inappropriate for the financial planner to not act, just like it would be inappropriate for the company to not act.

choices.text: Financial planners should advise their clients to save money for retirement only if retirement is many years away.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the manager’s conclusion, because it’s never stated. Furthermore, the conclusion is about the company, not about the financial planning situation—the analogy involving the financial planner forms the support for why it’s a bad idea to put off action just because an event is far in the future.

Worldwide, more books were sold last year than in any previous year. In particular, there were more cookbooks sold. For the first time ever, most of the cookbooks sold were not intended for beginners. Indeed, more cookbooks than ever were purchased by professional cooks. However, one of the few books available on every continent is a cookbook written for beginners, entitled Problem-Free Cooking.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.text: Last year there were more cookbooks sold that were not intended for beginners than in any previous year.
choices.rationale: Looking at this answer, it seems to be making an inference from statements #2 and 3. We do know that there were more cookbooks sold last year than ever before, and that, for the "first time ever" most of them weren't for beginners. Since previous years had fewer than half of the cookbooks sold targeted not at beginners, and fewer books were sold, last year having more books sold and most of them targeted at not beginners means that there were more of these books sold than any other year. This answer is supported by the information in the stimulus.

choices.text: The best-selling cookbook last year was a cookbook that was intended for beginners.
choices.rationale: There's no indication of what the best-selling book was, so this answer isn't supported.

choices.text: Sales of cookbooks intended for beginners were lower last year than in previous years.
choices.rationale: While sales of books targeted at beginners fell below the 50% mark of cookbooks sold last year for the first time ever, that could have come from a surge in sales of other books, not a decline in sales of beginners books. Selecting this answer would mean that you fell for a percent to amount flaw.

choices.text: Most of the cookbooks purchased last year that were not intended for beginners were purchased by professional cooks.
choices.rationale: While more cookbooks than ever were purchased by professional cooks, the majority of those non-beginner books could have been purchased by home cooks who have some skills. More than ever doesn't mean most.

choices.text: Problem-Free Cooking sold more copies last year than did any cookbook written for professional cooks.
choices.rationale: While PFC was available on every continent, there's no indication in the stimulus of how well it sold compared to other books, so this answer is out of scope.

In early 2003, scientists detected methane in the atmosphere of Mars. Methane is a fragile compound that falls apart when hit by the ultraviolet radiation in sunlight. So any methane in the Martian atmosphere must have been released into the atmosphere relatively recently.
stem: The argument relies on the assumption that

choices.text: Mars had no methane in its atmosphere prior to 2003
choices.rationale: This isn’t an assumption that’s necessary for the argument to work. If (A) were true, then it would guarantee the truth of the conclusion (as long as “recently” means since 2003), but we aren’t looking for a sufficient assumption; we’re looking for something that has to be true in order for the argument to work. The year could just as easily be 1999, and the argument would still work, so (A) doesn’t have to be true.

choices.text: all methane in the Martian atmosphere is eventually exposed to sunlight
choices.rationale: This is an assumption that’s necessary in order for the argument to work. To test it, suppose that (B) were false. What if there were some methane in the Martian atmosphere that’s never eventually exposed to sunlight? In that case, the argument would fall apart! It would be possible for there to be methane found in the Martian atmosphere that wasn’t released there relatively recently, since that methane could have just escaped the threat of sunlight for centuries (for example).

choices.text: methane cannot be detected until it has started to fall apart
choices.rationale: This isn’t an assumption that’s necessary for the argument to work. There’s no indication in the passage of any relationship between detection and degradation of methane.

choices.text: the methane that the scientists detected had been exposed to ultraviolet radiation
choices.rationale: This isn’t an assumption that’s necessary for the argument to work. Whether the methane that the scientists detected had or hadn’t been exposed to ultraviolet radiation isn’t relevant to determining how recently the methane had been released.

choices.text: methane in Earth's atmosphere does not fall apart as a result of exposure to ultraviolet radiation
choices.rationale: This isn’t an assumption that’s necessary for the argument to work. What happens in Earth’s atmosphere isn’t necessary (or even relevant) to an argument about what happens in Mars’s atmosphere.

Environmentalist: Pollution from gasoline burned by cars contributes to serious environmental problems. But the cost of these problems is not reflected in gasoline prices, and hence usually does not affect consumers' decisions about how much to drive. Heavier taxes on gasoline, however, would reflect this cost, and as a result consumers would pollute less.
stem: The environmentalist's statements, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.text: The cost of pollution from driving should not be reflected in the price of gasoline unless the amount of pollution produced would be reduced as a result.
choices.rationale: The Environmentalist doesn't state that lowering pollution is a necessary condition for having the price of gas reflect its (environmental) costs.

choices.text: Heavier taxes on gasoline would increase consumers' awareness of the kinds of environmental problems to which pollution from driving contributes.
choices.rationale: The Environmentalist does believe that higher taxes would result in less pollution, but that doesn't come from awareness of environmental problems—it comes from people using less gas since it costs more.

choices.text: Consumers would purchase less gasoline, on average, if the cost of the environmental problems to which pollution from driving contributes were fully reflected in the price of gasoline.
choices.rationale: This answer highlights the connection that the Environmentalist draws between higher taxes and less pollution. The cost of gas doesn't reflect environmental costs of pollution, and so it doesn't affect consumer decisions. Higher taxes would "result" in less pollution, thus justifying this answer.

choices.text: The only cost considered by most consumers when they are deciding how much to drive is the cost of gasoline.
choices.rationale: The Environmentalist states that the cost of gasoline is considered by consumers when considering how much to drive, but it's not laid out as the only consideration.

choices.text: Pollution from gasoline burned by cars will be reduced only if consumers give more consideration to the cost of that pollution when deciding how much to drive.
choices.rationale: While the Environmentalist believes that consumers giving more consideration to the cost of pollution will reduce that pollution, she never states that it's the only thing that can reduce pollution.

Hine's emerald dragonflies are an endangered species that live in wetlands. The larvae of these dragonflies can survive only in the water, where they are subject to predation by several species including red devil crayfish. Surprisingly, the dragonfly populations are more likely to remain healthy in areas where red devil crayfish are present than in areas without red devil crayfish.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the surprising fact?

choices.text: Red devil crayfish dig chambers that remain filled with water even when the surrounding wetlands dry up.
choices.rationale: This helps explain why dragonfly populations are likelier to remain healthy in areas with the crayfish than without. If (A) is true, it introduces a benefit (water, which dragonfly larvae need to survive) of the presence of red devil crayfish that may well offset the danger that that same presence introduces.

choices.text: Red devil crayfish present no threat to adult Hine's emerald dragonflies.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t help explain the situation, which is surprising because dragonfly larvae are in danger from red devil crayfish. If too many larvae were killed, we would expect the dragonfly population to be unhealthy—regardless of whether or not adult dragonflies are threatened.

choices.text: The varied diet of the red devil crayfish does not include any animal species that prey on dragonfly larvae.
choices.rationale: This actually makes the situation even more surprising. If the red devil crayfish did eat other predators of the dragonfly larvae, and those other predators were more dangerous to the larvae, then that could help explain why dragonfly populations are safer in the presence of one predator than without. But since (C) tells us that this isn’t the case, then the situation becomes even more puzzling—why do dragonfly populations do better in the presence of red devil crayfish?

choices.text: Red devil crayfish are found in many more locations than Hine's emerald dragonflies are.
choices.rationale: This comparison doesn’t explain the situation, because it’s not helpful to have information about how many places red devil crayfish are found in versus how many places the dragonflies are found in. The question is why dragonfly populations are healthier when they do overlap with red devil crayfish populations than when they don’t.

choices.text: Populations of red devil crayfish in a wetland do not drop significantly if the local population of Hine's emerald dragonflies dies out.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t help explain the situation, which is surprising because dragonfly larvae are in danger from red devil crayfish. What happens to populations of red devil crayfish if the dragonflies disappear doesn’t shed any light on the situation.

Stress is a common cause of high blood pressure. By calming their minds and thereby reducing stress, some people can lower their blood pressure. And most people can calm their minds, in turn, by engaging in exercise.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.text: For at least some people, having lower blood pressure has at least some tendency to cause their stress levels to be reduced.
choices.rationale: This answer reverses the established causal relationship, so it's incorrect.

choices.text: Most people with high blood pressure can lower their blood pressure by reducing their stress levels.
choices.rationale: This answer reflects the second sentence, which was said to apply to "some people," not most.

choices.text: Most people who do not exercise regularly have higher stress levels as a result.
choices.rationale: While exercise is noted as being one way to calm one's mind and thus lower stress levels, it doesn't establish it as the primary, only, or best way to do so, so people who don't exercise might still have low stress levels because they, say, meditate.

choices.text: Engaging in exercise can directly lower one's blood pressure.
choices.rationale: The stimulus establishes that exercise can help calm one's mind, and calming one's mind can lower stress, which can lower blood pressure. That's an indirect relationship, not a direct one.

choices.text: For at least some people, engaging in exercise can cause their stress levels to be reduced.
choices.rationale: While this answer doesn't use all the premises, it does reflect the causal chain that we developed. Exercise can calm the mind, which is stated as lowering stress, supporting this answer.

stimulus:
Question Prompt Passage

A positive correlation has been found between the amount of soot in the atmosphere of cities and the frequency of a certain ailment among those cities' populations. However, the soot itself probably does not cause this ailment, since in cities where there are large amounts of soot in the air, there are usually also high concentrations of many other air pollutants.
stem: Which one of the following statements, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: In cities where there are high concentrations of many air pollutants but little if any soot in the air, the frequency of the ailment is just as high, on average, as it is in cities where there are large amounts of soot in the air.
choices.rationale: This actually strengthens the argument, which concludes that soot by itself doesn’t cause the ailment. (A) provides information that suggests that the other air pollutants that often accompany soot actually cause the ailment also, and in the absence of soot. So, if (A) is true, it actually suggests that the air pollutants cause the ailment—that helps the passage’s argument that it’s not soot itself that causes the ailment.

choices.text: If the ailment rarely occurs except in cities in which there are large amounts of soot in the air, then the soot is probably the cause of the ailment.
choices.rationale: This condition doesn’t weaken the argument. It doesn’t actually add anything to the argument, since it doesn’t address the presence (or absence) of the other air pollutants in question. Additionally, the rarity of the ailment isn’t necessarily a factor in this argument, so (B)’s condition might never be triggered.

choices.text: In each of the cities where there are large amounts of soot in the air but little other air pollution, the frequency of the ailment is at least as high as it is anywhere else.
choices.rationale: This weakens the argument, which concludes that soot by itself doesn’t cause the ailment in question, because high amounts of soot are often accompanied by high amounts of other pollutants. If (C) is true, it provides information about places where soot is found without those other air pollutants, and the frequency of the ailment is essentially unaffected by that absence. That makes it more likely that soot alone can cause the ailment, which makes the passage’s conclusion less likely to follow from its support.

choices.text: If high concentrations of many different pollutants in a city's air are correlated with a high frequency of the ailment among that city's population, then it is possible that two or more of those pollutants each causally contributes to the ailment.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t weaken the argument. Like (B), this choice provides a condition that isn’t necessarily relevant to this argument—it might never be triggered, which would leave the argument unaffected.

choices.text: In cities in which there are high concentrations of many air pollutants, there are generally also high concentrations of other forms of pollution that are very likely to contribute causally to the ailment.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t weaken the argument. (E) states a correlation between air pollutants and other forms of pollution that cause the ailment, but that doesn’t shed any light on whether soot by itself can cause the ailment.

So far this summer there has been no rain in the valley. But usually a few inches of rain fall there each summer. Since only one week of summer is left, it will probably rain in the valley within the next week.
stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following arguments?

choices.text: Aisha has finished proofreading all but the last two pages of an issue of the journal Periodos and has encountered no errors. However, there are sometimes a few errors in an issue of the journal Periodos. So there may be errors in the pages that Aisha has not yet checked.
choices.rationale: This argument doesn’t have a flaw that matches the passage’s flaw. In fact, (A)’s argument is reasonable: it concludes that there may be errors based on the fact that there are sometimes a few errors. That doesn’t match the passage, which erroneously concludes that something will probably happen because it usually happens (and hasn’t happened yet).

choices.text: There are generally few errors in an issue of the journal Periodos. Aisha has finished proofreading all but the last two pages of an issue of this journal but has encountered no errors. Hence, there are probably no errors in the pages that Aisha has not yet checked in this issue of the journal.
choices.rationale: This argument doesn’t have a flaw that matches the passage’s flaw. A problem with (B)’s argument is that it concludes that there are probably no errors in the remaining pages, due to the fact that there are generally few (not many) errors. [Note that “few” isn’t the same as “a few.”] That doesn’t match the passage, which concludes that something will probably happen because it usually happens (and hasn’t happened yet).

choices.text: On average, there are a few errors in an issue of the journal Periodos. Aisha has finished proofreading all but the last two pages of an issue of this journal but has encountered no errors. So there are probably errors in the pages she has not yet checked in this issue of the journal.
choices.rationale: This argument has a flaw that matches the passage’s flaw. The passage erroneously concludes that something will probably happen just because it usually happens. (C) commits a similar flaw: it concludes that there are probably errors in the remaining pages just because there are on average (or, usually) a few errors in the journal as a whole.

choices.text: Aisha has proofread several issues of the journal Periodos and has encountered no errors. But there are seldom any errors in an issue of this journal. So there will probably be no errors in the next issue of the journal Periodos that she proofreads.
choices.rationale: This argument doesn’t have a flaw that matches the passage’s flaw. (D) concludes that there will probably be no errors based on the fact that there are seldom any errors. That doesn’t match the passage, which erroneously concludes that something will probably happen because it usually happens (and hasn’t happened yet).

choices.text: There usually are errors in each issue of the journal Periodos. Since Aisha has finished proofreading the latest issue of this journal and has detected no errors, Aisha has probably made a mistake in her proofreading.
choices.rationale: This argument doesn’t have a flaw that matches the passage’s flaw. (E) concludes that Aisha has probably made a mistake because she hasn’t detected any errors. That doesn’t match the passage, which concludes that something will probably happen because it usually happens (and hasn’t happened yet).

stimulus:
Question Prompt Passage

Young people believe efforts to reduce pollution, poverty, and war are doomed to failure. This pessimism is probably harmful to humanity's future, because people lose motivation to work for goals they think are unrealizable. We must do what we can to prevent this loss of motivation and therefore must enable our children to believe that better futures are possible.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?

choices.text: Motivating people to work to solve humanity's problems will enable them to believe that the future can be better and will cause them to be less pessimistic.
choices.rationale: This answer choice reverses the connection needed for the stimulus to work. The stimulus requires enabling people to view a better future as driving them to have motivation to change, not creating the motive in order to make people more optimistic.

choices.text: Enabling people to believe that better futures are possible will help prevent the loss of motivation that results from pessimistic beliefs about the future.
choices.rationale: This answer choice connects the proposed solution to the problem—making people more optimistic prevents a loss of motivation to make the world a better place. If enabling people to view a better future doesn't prevent that loss of motivation, then the proposed solution from the stimulus won't work to solve the problem.

choices.text: Optimism about the future is better than pessimism, even if that optimism is based on an illusory vision of what is likely to occur.
choices.rationale: The argument doesn't require one view to be "better" than another—just to lead to a certain outcome (motivation to make the world a better place).

choices.text: If future generations believe that the future can be better, then pollution, poverty, and war will be eliminated.
choices.rationale: The argument is about motivation and viewpoint, not actually solving these problems, so this answer is out of scope. Even when discussing these specific problems, it's framed as what young people "believe"—not whether they're actually solvable.

choices.text: The current prevalence of such problems as pollution and poverty stems from previous generations' inability to believe that futures can be better.
choices.rationale: The cause of the problems that young people view as unsolvable are out of scope of an argument about motivation to solve those problems.

stimulus:
Question Prompt Passage

In a recent study of stroke patients, those who exhibited continuing deterioration of the nerve cells in the brain after the stroke also exhibited the highest levels of the protein glutamate in their blood. Glutamate, which functions within nerve cells as a neurotransmitter, can kill surrounding nerve cells if it leaks from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells. Thus glutamate leaking from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells is a cause of long-term brain damage resulting from strokes.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.text: Any neurotransmitter that leaks from a damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cell will damage surrounding nerve cells.
choices.rationale: This actually weakens the argument. If any neurotransmitter that leaks from a damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cell will damage the nerve cells, then it might not be glutamate that’s causing the brain damage—and it could just be a coincidence that glutamate is present in the blood.

choices.text: Stroke patients exhibit a wide variety of abnormal chemical levels in their blood.
choices.rationale: This could actually weaken the argument. If (B) is true, then other chemical abnormalities—not glutamate—might actually be the cause of the brain damage.

choices.text: Glutamate is the only neurotransmitter that leaks from oxygen-starved or physically damaged nerve cells.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t strengthen the argument, though it’s sometimes tempting to students. Even if (C) is true, there could still be other proteins that cause the brain damage—proteins that come from somewhere other than oxygen-starved or physically damaged nerve cells. In other words, glutamate’s presence could still be completely coincidental to the brain damage.

choices.text: Leakage from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells is the only possible source of glutamate in the blood.
choices.rationale: This strengthens the argument, which concludes causation from a correlation. If (D) is true, and leakage from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells is the only way that glutamate could be found in the blood, then other potential reasons for glutamate’s presence are eliminated. That makes it more likely that glutamate is the cause of the brain damage. It doesn’t prove the argument’s truth, but it doesn’t have to—we’re asked to strengthen the argument, not prove it.

choices.text: Nerve cells can suffer enough damage to leak glutamate without being destroyed themselves.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t affect the argument, because the process of nerve cell damage isn’t relevant to whether the glutamate leaked from nerve cells is damaging to brain cells.

stimulus:
Question Prompt Passage

The only songs Amanda has ever written are blues songs and punk rock songs. Most punk rock songs involve no more than three chords. So if the next song Amanda writes is not a blues song, it probably will not involve more than three chords.
stem: The reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.text: The only pets the Gupta family has ever owned are fish and parrots. Most parrots are very noisy. So if the next pet the Gupta family owns is a parrot, it will probably be very noisy.
choices.rationale: This argument isn’t similar to the passage’s argument. stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?

choices.text: There has recently been increased demand at LargeCo stores for the chain's own brand of yogurt as well as for other brands of yogurt.
choices.rationale: This actually makes the discrepancy worse. choices.rationale: This helps resolve the discrepancy. If (D) is true, then yogurt sales are facing a significant challenge. Principle: One should never be insincere about one's feelings, except possibly where one believes that the person with whom one is speaking would prefer kindness to honesty.
stem: The principle, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments concerning the problem?

choices.text: If Shayna congratulates Daniel, she will avoid hurting his feelings, so she should congratulate him.
choices.rationale: The principle isn't about whether or not someone's feelings would be hurt, so this answer is out of scope.

choices.text: Daniel might prefer for Shayna to congratulate him—even if insincerely—rather than for her to express her true feelings, and so Shayna would be doing nothing wrong in insincerely congratulating Daniel.
choices.rationale: The principle is about what Shayna "believes" Daniel would prefer, so this answer about his actual preference is out of scope.

choices.text: Shayna believes that kindness should be preferred to dishonesty when speaking to others, so she should not tell Daniel her true feelings.
choices.rationale: The principle is about a speaker's belief about what the person being spoken to would prefer, so Shayna's preferences on kindness vs. honesty are out of scope.

choices.text: Daniel's feelings would be hurt if he knew that congratulations from Shayna were insincere, so Shayna should not congratulate him.
choices.rationale: First, this answer is about feelings being hurt, not preferences, so it's out of scope. Additionally, it doesn't establish what Shayne does or doesn't believe about Daniel's preferences, so it's out of scope again!

choices.text: Shayna has no opinion about whether Daniel would prefer kindness to honesty, so she should not congratulate him.
choices.rationale: However, the sufficient condition of the principle is that a speaker doesn't believe the listener would prefer kindness to honesty—that's subtly different from believing the listener wouldn't prefer kindness to honesty. Since this answer states that Shayna has no opinion on Daniel's preferences, she doesn't think that he'd prefer kindness to honesty, and so the principle applies—establishing that Shayna should be sincere. According to the problem, that means she shouldn't congratulate him.

stem: Which one of the following is an assumption the farmer's argument requires?

choices.rationale: This answer compares the harm to wildlife by GMO crops to that of insecticides, stating that they do less harm—a necessary assumption for the argument to work. choices.rationale: This answer is too extreme in stating that GMO crops are "never" sprayed with insecticides. While the argument relies on some GMO crops not being sprayed by insecticides, if they are sometimes sprayed, the argument could still work.

choices.rationale: The argument is about whether this shift would work if it happens, not if it's feasible to make happen. As such, the economics of it are out of scope.
